skeleton:
Salona — Sweet-Sour Fish of the Libyan Sabbath

Libyan · Medium · 6

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The salona is the Libyan Sephardic table's fish seat — whole fish or thick steaks braised in the sweet-sour pan of onions, honey, and vinegar, the vegetables cut large and cooked to the syrup's gilding. It is the #64 chraime's sister craft at the opposite dial: where the chraime runs the spice's fire, the salona runs the agrodolce's sweetness — the same Rosh Hashanah-and-Sabbath logic that runs the #80 marqa batata, aimed at the sea.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

- **The salona's law: the fish braises in the syrup's body, never boils in its broth.** The vegetables cook down to the thick, glossy sweet-sour base first — the liquid reduced to a clinging sauce — and only then the fish enters, to poach gently through its few minutes. The fish's patience is the record's whole hinge: the long-simmered fish runs dry and the Sabbath's finest turns to sawdust. - **The bridge:** the #64 chraime and this record share the Sephardic fish-in-pan doctrine — the one pot, the sauce built, the fish laid in — split at the dial: fire versus sweet. The #80's agrodolce law (the vinegar and honey in balance, never contest) carries here unchanged.

Salona — Sweet-Sour Fish of the Libyan Sabbath

Prep: 25 min · Cook: 45 min · Total: 1 h 10 min · 6

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 1.2 kg whole white fish (grouper, sea bass, or hake), cleaned, in 5 cm steaks, or 6 fillets (about 800 g)
  • 3 tbsp olive oil (about 40 g)
  • 3 onions (about 600 g), halved and sliced thick
  • 4 garlic cloves, crushed
  • 2 carrots (about 200 g), in thick coins
  • 1 celery stalk with leaves, in 4 cm lengths
  • 2 tomatoes (about 250 g), grated
  • 3 tbsp red wine vinegar (about 45 ml)
  • 2 tbsp honey or sugar (about 40 g honey)
  • 1 tsp salt, more to taste
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • ¼ tsp saffron threads (about 0.3 g), bloomed in 2 tbsp warm water, optional but the Sabbath's own
  • 250 ml water
  • The finish: lemon juice and chopped parsley

Instructions

  1. **The sweet-sour base (30 minutes).** The oil in the wide pan over medium; the onions, carrots, and celery cooked with the salt, covered, 15 minutes to the deep soften, then uncovered 10 minutes more to the gilding's start — the fond building at the pan's floor. The garlic, tomatoes, turmeric, and saffron's bloom in; the vinegar and honey stirred through, and the water added to the vegetables' half-height. The pan simmered 10 minutes, uncovered, to the thickened, glossy sauce. Checkpoint — the base's proof: the sauce clings to the spoon's back, the carrots tender at the knife's tip yet holding their coin's shape, the taste a balance of bright and round — sharper than the #80's potato pot (the fish wants the vinegar's edge against its richness) but neither contestant drowning the other.
  2. **The fish's entry (12–15 minutes).** The steaks laid into the sauce in one layer, the spoon's sauce ladled over their backs, the pan covered and the heat dropped to the barest simmer — the surface barely shivering, an 85 °C order of gentleness — until the flesh turns just-opaque at the bone's seam (12 minutes for the 5 cm steak, 8 for the fillet). Checkpoint — the fish's law at the bone: the tip of the knife at the spine's seam shows opaque flesh that parts from the bone's own gloss with no resistance — the translucent heart of the undercooked or the dry flake's crumbling of the overdone are both failures; the salona's fish must be at the exact edge, because the carryover in the warm sauce finishes the last degree.
  3. **The rest and the service.** The pan rested off the heat 10 minutes, the lemon juice's brightness and the parsley's green folded at the edge — the salona served warm, never hot, with the bread for the sauce and the vegetables mounded alongside. Checkpoint — eating test: the fish's sweet flake in the glossy, sweet-sour coat — the onion's silk and the carrot's gilded coin on the same bread-swept spoon — the vinegar's brightness cutting the fish's oil, the honey rounding the saffron's sea-air. It should taste like the Libyan Sabbath's own argument — the sea and the garden, one pot, the year's sweetness asked over both.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Fish dry, flaking to crumbsThe simmer's rush or the clock's excessThe 85 °C shiver; the bone's-seam law
Sauce thin at the fish's entryThe base's reduction rushedThe cling-to-spoon proof before the fish enters
Sauce one-note sharpThe vinegar unharnessedThe honey's dial upward; the rest's mellowing

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The base keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves — the Friday-make law is the record's own inheritance; the fish, once poached, keeps one day only, gently reheated in the warm sauce, never the boil. The variations: the whole-fish Sabbath presentation (the head's own blessing at Rosh Hashanah), the spicier Tripoli dial (a spoon of the #91 harissa in the base), the artichoke's spring seat under the same syrup.
